title: Hardware fingerprint heatmap + driver coupling notes
content:
Summary:
This notes doc records a targeted set of hardware comparison experiments intended to build a compact fingerprint (heatmap) for how A100 / H100 / L40S behave across cloud SKUs when we vary CUDA and driver stacks and workload patterns commonly seen by our runtime. The intent is not exhaustive coverage but to capture systematic coupling: which driver/CUDA combos amplify tail latency, which amplify throughput variance under mixed batches, and where NVLink vs PCIe locality shows up in our decode and KV-cache heavy workloads.

Key experimental goals:
- Produce a small, visual-friendly heatmap (described below) that maps p50/p95/p99 latency deltas and decode throughput deltas across sku x driver x cuda combos.
- Identify reproducible tail-latency fingerprints that correlate with driver versions or firmware.
- Generate hypotheses for mitigation (kernel selection, prewarming, placement) and produce immediate config recommendations for Dedicated clusters.

Testbed & workloads:
- Models: 7B transformer (prefill+decode), 70B transformer (prefill heavy), long-context 16k-ish refill test.
- Typical requests: small-batch interactive (1-4 requests, decode length 64), batching workload (packed dynamic batches up to 32), KV-cache re-use scenario (many short queries with warm cache).
- Cloud SKUs included (representative names):
  - AWS: p4d.24xlarge (A100 40GB/80GB variants we had), p5.24xlarge (H100)
  - GCP: a2-highgpu-1g (A100), a3-highgpu-1g (H100), l40s-preview (L40S)
  - Azure: ND A100-series and ND H100-preview (labels obfuscated for notes)
- Node config: same docker runtime, same container image built from main branch commit referenced in linked_artifacts, pinned pytorch 2.x + triton baseline where used.
- Driver/CUDA matrix sampled: CUDA 11.8, 12.1, 12.2; Drivers: 520.xx, 535.xx, 545.xx (where available). We also toggled MPS and MIG (A100 only) in a subset.
- Telemetry: token-level latency events, kernel launch timestamps, PCIe/NVLink counters, host CPU utilization, eBPF traces for task scheduling where possible.

Observations (high level):
1) Tail amplification under mixed small batches:
   - H100 nodes showed the most sensitivity to driver patchlevel when mixing prefill-heavy requests and low-latency interactive requests. On CUDA 12.1 + driver 535.x we observed p99 spikes 2.4x higher than same SKU on driver 545.xx for the same workload; direction suggests a runtime launch-path change in the older driver induced queueing.
   - A100 nodes were more stable across driver versions but exhibited higher baseline p50 under heavy NVLink utilization. When a neighbor process saturated NVLink for large prefill transfers, our decode p95 moved up ~15–20ms consistently.

2) L40S behaviour (thermal cadence + clock governor):
   - L40S showed good steady-state throughput for long-context workloads but exhibited time-dependent drift in throughput/p99 after sustained 20+ minute sessions on some cloud images. We correlated this to a firmware thermal cadence (clock governors cycling) on a subset of instances; updating host image kernel and driver to 545.xx reduced amplitude of drift.

3) PCIe vs NVLink locality effects:
   - Workloads with host-to-GPU large prefill data (long prompt loads) had markedly different decode tail depending on whether the model weights and KV were colocated on the same GPU with NVLink vs needing PCIe hops. Nonlocal paths added jitter that manifested at p95/p99 but not at p50.

4) KV-cache eviction and memory fragmentation fingerprint:
   - A100 with older drivers produced more frequent small allocations that led to higher transient OOM-recovery latency when we simulated aggressive KV churn; newer drivers with improved allocator paths (545 series) resulted in smoother eviction profiles.

Detailed result sketch (compact heatmap description):
- Heatmap axes: rows=SKUs (A100, H100, L40S * cloud flavor), cols=driver+CUDA combos (11.8/520, 12.1/535, 12.2/545).
- Cell values: three short tags separated by pipe: p50_delta_ms|p95_delta_ms|tokens_per_sec_delta_pct relative to baseline cell (A100 on 12.2+545). Example cell: "+4|+18|-7%" (p50 +4ms, p95 +18ms, throughput -7%).
- Notable cells: H100@12.1/535: "+6|+40|-18%" for 70B mixed workloads. L40S@11.8/520: "+2|+12|-5%" but with time drift noted. A100@12.2/545: baseline "0|0|0%" for reference.

Reproducible anomalies and follow-ups:
- Replica: On p5 (H100) with CUDA 12.1/driver 535 we could reproduce a bursty kernel queue backlog when concurrent prefill transfers were active. Reproduced on two cloud regions — filing as likely driver-launch/stream scheduling coupling. Action: open driver-telemetry PR + vendor bug report (attached to JIRA-RT-4823).
- L40S drift only reproduced on certain machine images; kernel and distro variant mattered. Action: standardize host images for Dedicated L40S pools and add thermal-clock telemetry.
- Mis-attribution risk: certain spikes coincident with host CPU steal on multi-tenant instances; verified by isolating runs on single-tenant (dedicated) nodes — tail behavior persisted on H100 but was reduced on A100, indicating both host and firmware interplay.

Quick mitigations we validated (practical recommendations):
- For Dedicated capacity serving latency-sensitive interactive traffic: prefer H100 nodes only if driver stack is updated to 545.x (or latest vendor-stable). Add node preflight that checks kernel/driver combination and auto-blocks older combos from release ring.
- For mixed workloads on A100: prefer NVLink-local placement for prefill-heavy requests (co-scheduling inference and KV-resident tasks) — the runtime should prefer placement hints when model partitioning is colocated.
- For L40S: schedule long-context batch jobs on nodes with validated host images; add rolling thermal-check in node health probe.
- Runtime knobs: precreate persistent CUDA streams and warm kernel caches on startup for model sizes that experienced launch stalls; enable conservative allocation patterns under heavy KV churn to avoid frequent allocator paths that spike tail.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Quantify impact of MPS (multi-process service) on tail for small-batch interactive traffic on H100: initial runs disabled MPS; we should run a sparse matrix enabling MPS with controlled sandboxing.
- Deeper kernel-level attribution: capture cupti traces alongside eBPF to map GPU kernel launch latencies to host call stacks to determine whether the backlog is on our side (host enqueue) or driver side (internal reordering).
- Expand heatmap to include firmware versions and BIOS/host kernel variants (we saw L40S sensitivity) — nontrivial to catalog but necessary for Private customers.

Appendix (notes to reproduce):
- Repro steps for the H100 bursty backlog:
  1) Start a steady prefill generator: repeated 3–5 second large prompt prefill to saturate NVLink for 60s.
  2) Start 8 concurrent interactive small requests (len=32) with 0.2s arrival jitter.
  3) Pin container to exclusive GPU mode, run on CUDA 12.1 + 535.xx driver, capture token-level traces and nvprof/cupti traces.
  4) Observe kernel enqueue latencies (host timestamp to device start) and check for 10–50ms backlog spikes aligning with p99 events.
- Useful artifacts: saved perf profiles in s3://redwood-bench/hw-fingerprint/2024-11-h100-535 (referenced from JIRA ticket).

Conclusion:
This targeted fingerprinting exercise surfaced clear driver/CUDA coupling effects, a thermal/firmware cadence on L40S images, and placement-sensitive NVLink/PCIe tail behaviors. Next steps are prioritized: file vendor bug reports for H100 backlog, standardize L40S host images, and bake a lightweight preflight driver/hardware check into Dedicated node provisioning.

Notes-to-self: convert heatmap into a single-page PDF with color legend and include a small reproducible script under serving-runtime/tools/hw-fingerprint that coordinates the prefill + interactive harness (open PR referenced in linked_artifacts).
